translations.text: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine,
and the fragrance of your ointments is better than all fragrances. Your name is ointment poured out; that is why the maidens have loved you.

They have drawn you; let us run after you toward the fragrance of your ointment. The bride tells the maidens what her mother granted her: "The king has brought me into his treasury; let us rejoice and be glad in you." The bride tells the maidens, and they said: "We have loved your breasts more than wine. Uprightness has loved you." The maidens call the bridegroom by name.
I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the dwellings of Kedar and like the tent of Solomon.
Do not look at me because I have grown dark, for the sun has disregarded me. My mother's sons fought against me; they set me as keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I did not keep."

The bride says to the bridegroom: "Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where do you pasture your flock? Where do you make them lie down at noon? Or else you may become like one who gathers in the flocks of others.
If you do not know yourself, fair one among women, go out in the tracks of your flocks and pasture your kids by the dwellings of the shepherds.
I have likened you to my horse among Pharaoh's chariots, my companion.
Your cheeks have become beautiful like a turtledove's, and your neck like strung beads.
We will liken you to a work of gold and to finely studded silver.
And the king put his hands around you. The bride speaks about herself and the bridegroom: "My nard has given out its fragrance.
My beloved is to me a bound bundle of myrrh; he will rest among my bridal things [?].
My beloved is to me a blossoming cluster in the vineyard of Engedi."
The bridegroom speaks to the bride: "Look, you are beautiful, my companion; look, your eyes are beautiful, like a dove's.
Look, you are good, my beloved; there is shade over my bed.
The beams of my house are of fir, and the rafters are of cypress."
The bridegroom speaks about himself and the bride: "I am a flower of the field, a lily of the valleys.
Like a lily among thorns, so is my companion among the daughters.
Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. I longed for his shade and sat down under it, and his fruit is sweet to my taste."
The bride says to the maidens: "Bring me into the house of wine; set love in order over me.
Strengthen me with the fragrance of ointments; surround me with apples, for I am wounded with love."
The bridegroom says to the bride: "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.
I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: when it rises, awaken love, whenever it wishes.
The voice of my beloved: "Look, here he comes, leaping on the mountains and running on the hills.

My beloved is like a gazelle and like a fawn of the deer on the mountains of Bethel." The bride tells the maidens about the bridegroom: "Look, there he is behind our wall, looking in through the window, through the lattices."
My beloved answers me and says to me: "Arise, come, my beautiful one, my dove.
For behold, the winter has passed; the rain has ceased and gone.
Flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.
The fig tree has put forth its blossom; our vines are in flower and have given off their fragrance." The bridegroom says to the bride: "Arise, come, my close companion, my dove.
In the shade beneath the rock, near the wall, show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet to hear and your face is beautiful to see."
The bridegroom says to the maidens: "Catch for us the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in flower."
My beloved is mine and I am his, he who pastures his flock among the lilies.
Until the day passes and the shadow comes, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young deer on the fragrant mountains.
On my bed at night I sought him whom my soul loved;
I called him, but he did not answer me; I sought him, but I did not find him.
The watchmen who go about the city found me. "Have you perhaps found him whom my soul loves?"

I had gone only a little past them when I found him whom my soul loves." The bride found the bridegroom and said: "I seized him and will not let him go until I have brought him into my mother's house, into the treasure-chambers of the one who bore me.
I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the strengths of the field: if you rouse and awaken it, let it be when it pleases."
The bridegroom asks the bride: "Who is this coming up from the wilderness, rising like a column of incense smoke? Myrrh and frankincense and every blend of the perfume-makers."
The maidens said this: "Behold, here is Solomon's couch, with sixty mighty men around it, from the mighty men of Israel.
All of them have swords in their hands and are trained for battle, each man with his sword at his thigh because of fear by night.
King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon.
He made its pillars of silver, its arched back of gold, its seat of purple; its floor was set with carbuncle, out of love for the daughters of Jerusalem.
Go out and see King Solomon; look at the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of his gladness."

The bridegroom spoke thus: "Behold, there you stand, my close companion; behold, there you stand, my beautiful one. Your eyes are doves' eyes, apart from your silence. Your hair is like a flock of goats that appeared from Edom.
Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes coming up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and there is not a barren one among them.
Your lips are scarlet, as if dyed with crimson, a covering of a single thread [?], and your speech is beautiful. Like the rind of a pomegranate are your cheeks, apart from your silence.
Your neck is like the tower of David; a thousand shields hang on it, and all the arrows of the mighty men.
Your two breasts are like twin fawns of a gazelle that graze among the lilies.
Until the day dawns and the shadows move, I myself will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of Lebanon.
You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.

Come here from Lebanon, bride; come from the place of frankincense. You will come and pass over the summit of Arveta, over the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dwellings of lions and from the mountains of leopards.
You have made our heart long for you, our sister, bride. You have set us on fire with a single strand of your necklace beads.
How lovely your breasts have become, my sister, bride. How much more beautiful your breasts are than wine, and the scent of your garments is better than all spices.
Your lips drip honey, my sister, bride. Honey and milk are under your tongue, and the scent of your garments is like the scent of frankincense.
My sister, the bride, is a guarded garden, a guarded garden, a sealed spring.
What you send forth is a fruitful paradise, a fruit-bearing tree, henna with nard.
Nard and saffron, incense, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes, with all precious spices.
A spring of paradise and a source of living water, flowing out of Lebanon.
Awake, south wind, and come, north wind! Blow on my garden and let the fragrance of my spices flow out. Let my beloved come down into his garden and eat of his fruits.

"I have come into my garden, my sister, bride! I have gathered my myrrh with my spices. I have eaten my bread with my honey, and I have drunk my wine with my milk." The bridegroom says to the companions: "Eat, companions, and drink, and become drunk, my beloved ones."

"I sleep, but my soul is awake." The bride hears the bridegroom knocking at the door and says: "The voice of my beloved is knocking at the door: 'Open, my beloved, my dove, my bride! My head is soaked with the dew of the night.'"
I have taken off my garment. How can I put it on again? I have washed my feet. How can I make them dirty?
My dear beloved put his hand in through the opening, and my insides stirred for him.
I got up to open the door to my beloved. My hands dripped myrrh, and my fingers were full of myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.
I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had gone away from me, and my soul went out at his word. I looked for him and did not find him. I called him, and he did not answer me.
The watchmen who go around the city found me. They beat me and wounded me. The watchmen of the wall took my garment from me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the strengths of the field: if we find my beloved, what will you tell him? For I am wounded with love.
"How is your beloved better than any other beloved, most beautiful among women? How is your beloved better than any other beloved, that you make us swear this way?"
The bride says to them: "My beloved is radiant and ruddy, chosen from among the offspring of tens of thousands.
His head is gold of Uphaz. His locks are like the [?] tree, black as a raven.
His eyes are like doves' eyes beside full waters.
His cheeks are like bowls of spices that give off fragrant ointment. His lips are like lilies, dripping with fragrant perfumed ointments.
His hands are of gold, finely cut, full of gold of Tarshish. His belly is like ivory, inlaid with sapphire stones.
His legs are of marble, set firmly on bases of gold. He looks like Lebanon, like a choice fir tree.
His throat is full of sweetness and altogether desirable. This is my beloved, O daughters of Jerusalem."
The daughters ask her: "Where has your beloved gone, O fairest among women? Where has your beloved turned? We will seek him with you."
The bride answers: "My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock in the garden and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine, he who pastures his flock among the lilies.
You are lovely, my companion, like good pleasure, beautiful as Jerusalem, wondrous as armies drawn up in array.
Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me take flight. Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead;
your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes coming up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and there is no barren one among them;
your lips are crimson, as if dyed with a [?] cord, dyed of a single thread, and your speech is lovely; like the rind of a pomegranate is your beauty, beyond that silence of yours.
There are sixty queens and forty concubines.
My dove, my bride, is one; she is the only one of her mother. The maidens saw her and called her blessed, and the queens and concubines praised her.
Who is this who comes up like the dawn, beautiful, and like the moon, chosen, like the sun, wondrously arrayed?"

The bridegroom said: "I went down into the walnut garden to look at the fruits of the springs, to see whether the pomegranates were in bloom, or whether the fir tree had put forth shoots." The bride says to the bridegroom: "There I will give you my breasts.
And he set me like the chariot of Aminadab. My soul did not know it."
The bridegroom says to the maidens and the queens: "What will you see in the Shulammite, who comes like a company of camps?"
The bridegroom says to the bride: "How beautiful are your steps, O daughter of Aminadab! The graceful form of your thighs is like [?] beads, the work of a craftsman's hands;
your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking mixed wine; your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies;
your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle;
your neck is like a tower of ivory; your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon, at the gates among many daughters; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon that faces Damascus;
your head upon you is like Carmel; the braiding of your hair is like purple, like a king crowned with radiance in the arena.
How beautiful you are, and how sweet, O love, among delights!
Your stature is like a palm tree, and your bridal charms are like its clusters.
And I said: 'I will climb up this palm tree and take hold of its top.' Let your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your gums like apples,
and your palate like fragrant wine." The bride says to him: "You go after my beloved in uprightness, enough for my lips and teeth.
I am my beloved's, and his turning is toward me.
Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field; let us lodge in the villages;
Let us rise early and go to the vineyards. Let us see whether the vines have blossomed, whether the fir [?] has sprouted, whether the pomegranates are in flower. There I will give you my breasts.
The mandrakes have given off their fragrance, and at our doors are all the fruit-bearing trees, new with old, which my mother gave me. My beloved, I have kept them for you.
Who would let my beloved suck at my mother's breasts? Then if I found you outside, I would love you, and no one would despise me.

I would take hold of you and bring you into my mother's house and into the treasure chambers of the one who bore me. I would give you the perfumers' spiced wine to drink, and I would hand you the [?] (juice?) of my pomegranates.
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.
I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field: when you rise, awaken love only when it wishes."

The daughters and the queens said to the bridegroom: "Under the apple tree I awakened you. Love is like death. Jealousy is as cruel as hell. Its wings are wings of fire, of its flame. There the one who bore you was in labour with you,
for it is mighty.
Many waters cannot quench love, and rivers will not sweep it away. If a man gave his whole living for love, he would be utterly despised."
The daughters of Jerusalem say this: "Our sister is small and has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken for?
If she were a wall, we would carve her with boards of fir."
The bride says openly: "You would have built [?] silver battlements, or if she were a door... I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. I was before his eyes as one who found peace.
Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon, and he gave that vineyard to keepers. Each man would bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.
My vineyard is before me. The thousand is Solomon's, and two hundred go to those who keep its fruit."
The bride says: "You who sit in the gardens, companions are waiting for you. Let me hear your voice.
Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices."
